lessons.title: Designing Farrowing and Nursery Units
lessons.body: A farrowing unit is where sows give birth and nurse piglets. It must be dry, warm, and safe for both mother and piglets. In Africa, many farmers use simple pens made from locally available materials like timber, bamboo, or concrete blocks. The floor should be smooth but not slippery, with a slope of 1-2% towards a drain. Each farrowing pen should be at least 2.5 meters by 2 meters, with a creep area for piglets that is heated to 30-32Â°C for the first week. Use a heat lamp or a wooden box with a lid and a 100-watt bulb. The sow needs a resting area that is cool, around 18-20Â°C, so provide shade and ventilation. A farrowing crate can reduce piglet crushing, but if not available, use a rail around the pen walls 20-25 cm from the floor to give piglets an escape zone. The nursery unit is for weaned piglets, typically from 4 to 10 weeks old. Keep them in groups of 10-15, with 0.3-0.4 square meters per piglet. The floor should be easy to clean, such as concrete with a slight slope to a urine drain. Provide a warm sleeping area at 26-28Â°C and a cooler dunging area. Use solid dividers between pens to prevent drafts and disease spread. Ensure there is a footbath at the entrance and hand-washing station. Natural lighting is good, but avoid direct sunlight that can overheat. In hot climates, orient the building east-west to reduce sun exposure on the long sides. Use local materials like mud bricks, thatch, or corrugated iron, but ensure they are predator-proof and secure. Always include a small storage area for feed and tools within the unit to reduce movement in and out. Clean and disinfect between batches to break disease cycles.

lessons.title: Constructing Grow-Finish Barns
lessons.body: Grow-finish barns house pigs from about 10 weeks old until market weight, usually 90-110 kg. These pigs need more space: 0.8-1.0 square meters per pig in a fully slatted system, or 1.2-1.5 square meters in a bedded system. In Africa, many use open-sided barns with deep litter or concrete floors. The floor should be concrete, at least 10 cm thick, with a 2% slope to a drain. For deep litter, use dry sawdust, wood shavings, or chopped straw, and add fresh material weekly. The walls can be low (1.2 meters) with wire mesh above for ventilation. The roof should be high (3-4 meters at the eaves) and insulated with thatch or reflective material to reduce heat. In hot climates, consider a ridge vent and open sides. In cooler highland areas, use curtains that can be rolled down. Provide 15-20 cm of trough space per pig for feeding, and one water nipple for every 10-15 pigs. Group pigs by size to reduce fighting. Stocking density is critical: overcrowding leads to poor growth, tail biting, and disease. A common mistake is to keep too many pigs in a small space. For a 20-pig pen, you need at least 24 square meters. Build a loading ramp at one end for easy transport to market. Use local materials like eucalyptus poles, bamboo, and mud bricks to cut costs, but ensure the structure is strong enough to withstand wind and rain. Always include a concrete apron around the barn to prevent mud and rodents. Clean the barn daily, removing wet bedding and manure. Disinfect weekly with a 2% caustic soda solution or commercial disinfectant. Keep records of feed intake and weight gain to monitor performance.

lessons.title: Ventilation and Temperature Control Systems
lessons.body: Pigs are sensitive to heat. Unlike humans, they cannot sweat effectively, so they need help to stay cool. The ideal temperature for a grow-finish pig is 18-22Â°C, for a lactating sow 18-20Â°C, and for piglets 30-32Â°C in the first week. In hot African climates, temperatures often exceed 35Â°C, causing heat stress. Signs include panting, reduced feed intake, and poor growth. To control temperature, use natural ventilation: open-sided buildings with high roofs, ridge vents, and large openings on the prevailing wind side. For every 10 pigs, provide at least 0.5 square meters of inlet area and 0.3 square meters of outlet area. If natural ventilation is not enough, use fans. A 50-cm diameter fan can move 10,000 cubic meters of air per hour, enough for 50-60 grow-finish pigs. In very hot areas, use evaporative cooling pads or foggers. A simple fogger system uses nozzles that spray fine water droplets; this can lower temperature by 5-10Â°C. For piglets, provide a heated creep area with a heat lamp or a wooden box with a 100-watt bulb. In cold highland areas, use curtains, deep bedding, and maybe a small stove, but ensure carbon monoxide does not build up. Always monitor temperature with a simple thermometer at pig level. Humidity should be 50-70%; too high causes respiratory problems, too low causes dust. Ventilation also removes ammonia and moisture. Ammonia levels should be below 20 ppm; if your eyes water when you enter, it's too high. Use a simple ammonia detector or your nose. Adjust ventilation by opening or closing curtains, vents, or doors. In deep litter systems, ventilation is critical to keep litter dry. Stir litter weekly and add fresh material. During the rainy season, ensure drainage to avoid flooding. In all cases, provide shade and plenty of cool drinking water.

lessons.title: Waste Management and Manure Handling
lessons.body: A pig produces about 4-6 kg of manure per day, which is a valuable resource but also a potential pollutant. In Africa, many farmers use pig manure to fertilize crops, but it must be handled properly to avoid disease and flies. The first step is to collect manure daily. In concrete-floor barns, scrape or flush manure into a drain that leads to a collection pit. In deep litter systems, remove wet litter and add fresh bedding. The collection pit should be concrete, covered, and located away from the barn to reduce odors and flies. For liquid manure, use a biogas digester. A simple plastic bag digester or fixed-dome digester can produce biogas for cooking and lighting. For a 10-pig farm, a 6-cubic-meter digester can produce enough gas for 2-3 hours of cooking per day. The effluent from the digester is a rich fertilizer. If you don't have a digester, compost the manure. Mix manure with crop residues like maize stalks or rice straw, and turn the pile every week. After 4-6 weeks, it becomes compost. For solid manure, you can also dry it and sell it as organic fertilizer. Never dump manure into rivers or streams; it causes water pollution and spreads diseases. Also, avoid spreading fresh manure on fields; it can burn plants and spread parasites. Store manure in a covered area to prevent rain from washing nutrients away. Use gloves and boots when handling manure, and wash hands after. Keep the manure storage area away from the pig barn (at least 30 meters) to reduce flies and disease transmission. In intensive systems, consider a lagoon for liquid waste, but ensure it is lined to prevent groundwater contamination. Regularly check for leaks and repair. Good waste management also reduces odors, which improves neighbor relations and pig health.

lessons.title: Biosecurity Infrastructure and Layout
lessons.body: Biosecurity means keeping diseases out of your farm. The layout of your pig housing is your first line of defense. Start with a perimeter fence at least 1.5 meters high to keep out people and animals. The entrance should have a gate with a lock and a sign saying 'No Entry Without Permission'. Provide a footbath at the entrance of each building: a shallow concrete basin filled with disinfectant (e.g., 2% caustic soda or commercial virucide). Change the disinfectant daily. Also, have a hand-washing station with soap and water. If possible, have a changing room where workers and visitors put on farm-specific boots and coveralls. The layout should follow a flow: from clean to dirty. That means the feed storage and nursery should be at the entrance, and the grow-finish and sick pens at the back. Never move from sick pens to healthy pens without changing clothes and boots. Keep different age groups in separate buildings at least 10 meters apart. This prevents disease spread between batches. Use solid walls between pens to prevent nose-to-nose contact. For new pigs, have a quarantine pen at least 50 meters from the main herd. Quarantine for 30 days and monitor for signs of disease. Keep feed in closed bins to prevent rodents and birds. Control flies with screens and traps. Dispose of dead pigs immediately by burning or deep burial (at least 1 meter deep) away from water sources. Keep records of all visitors and their contact with pigs. In African contexts, many farms are small and mixed with other livestock; keep pigs separate from poultry and cattle if possible. If you have a vehicle, park it outside the fence. Always wash and disinfect boots and equipment after use. A simple biosecurity plan can save you from devastating diseases like African Swine Fever, for which there is no vaccine.

lessons.title: Equipment for Feeding and Watering
lessons.body: Pigs need constant access to clean water and feed. For watering, the simplest method is a nipple drinker connected to a tank. Each nipple serves 10-15 pigs. Nipples should be placed at shoulder height of the pigs: for weaners at 30 cm, for growers at 45 cm, and for finishers at 60 cm. Check water flow daily; a pig drinks 5-10 liters per day, more in hot weather. Use a water tank of at least 100 liters for 10 pigs, and clean it weekly. For feeding, you can use troughs or self-feeders. Troughs are cheaper but require more labor. A concrete trough 30 cm wide and 15 cm deep can feed 10 pigs; allow 20-30 cm of trough space per pig. Feed twice daily, and remove leftovers to prevent spoilage. Self-feeders save labor and reduce waste. A simple wooden or metal hopper with a trough at the bottom can hold 50 kg of feed. Adjust the opening so feed flows freely but doesn't spill. For piglets, use creep feeders with small openings. Always provide feed on a clean surface; never feed on the floor where manure is. In Africa, you can make feeders from local materials like clay pots, wooden planks, or PVC pipes. For example, cut a PVC pipe lengthwise and attach it to a wooden frame. For water, you can use a plastic drum with nipples. Ensure all equipment is easy to clean and disinfect. Remove feed leftovers daily to prevent mold. Store feed in a dry, cool place, off the floor on pallets, to prevent aflatoxin. Use a simple scale to weigh feed for accurate rationing. Keep records of feed intake per pen to detect health issues early. Clean water and proper feeding equipment are the backbone of good pig performance.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Housing and Facilities for Pig Farming in Africa

Housing is the single largest capital investment in a pig enterprise after breeding stock. In most African production systems â from smallholder units in Uganda to commercial operations in South Africa and Nigeria â poor housing accounts for 30â40% of pre-weaning mortality, reduced feed conversion, and respiratory disease losses. This practical reference gives you the numbers, layouts, and materials you need to build facilities that pay for themselves through lower mortality, faster growth, and reduced labour.

Design principles for the African context: use locally available materials (murram, clay bricks, treated eucalyptus, galvanised iron), prioritise natural ventilation over mechanical cooling, build for heat stress rather than cold stress, and phase construction so that revenue from the first batch funds the next unit.

Designing Farrowing and Nursery Units

The farrowing unit is the highest-value space on the farm â each sow weans 8â12 piglets per cycle, and a 1Â°C drop below 25Â°C in the creep area can cost you 1â2 piglets per litter. Build farrowing pens 2.4 m Ã 1.8 m (4.3 mÂ²) with a creep area of 0.6 mÂ² heated to 30â32Â°C for the first week, dropping to 26Â°C by weaning at 21â28 days. In African conditions, use a raised wooden or concrete creep floor with a 100 W infrared lamp or a locally fabricated heat pad â not a heat lamp in an open pen, which wastes energy and creates fire risk.

Nursery units (weaner to 10 weeks) should be 0.3 mÂ² per pig at 8 kg, rising to 0.5 mÂ² at 25 kg. Group size of 15â20 pigs per pen reduces aggression. Build nursery pens with solid floors and a 2% slope to a shallow drain for easy washing â slatted floors in nurseries increase respiratory disease risk in dusty African conditions.

Constructing Grow-Finish Barns

Grow-finish barns should be 8â10 m wide and up to 60 m long, with a ridge height of 3.5â4 m to allow hot air to escape. Orient the barn eastâwest in hot climates to reduce direct solar gain on the long walls. Use a 1:6 roof pitch with a 30â40 cm open ridge and 1.2 m roll-up side curtains. Floor: concrete, 8â10 cm thick, with a 2% slope to a central or side drain. In high-rainfall areas (Uganda, Cameroon), raise the floor 30â45 cm above ground and build a 1 m perimeter drainage channel.

Cost benchmarks from African commercial builds (2022â2024): a 100-pig grow-finish barn costs USD 8,000â14,000 in Kenya, USD 6,000â10,000 in Nigeria, and USD 10,000â18,000 in South Africa, depending on materials. Locally fired clay bricks and treated eucalyptus trusses cut costs by 25â35% versus imported steel.

Ventilation and Temperature Control Systems

Natural ventilation is the default for African pig housing. Minimum ventilation rate for grow-finish pigs is 0.6 mÂ³/min per pig in hot weather and 0.15 mÂ³/min in cool weather. In the tropics, target an air exchange rate of 30â60 air changes per hour in summer. Use open-ridge barns with side curtains, ceiling fans (1 fan per 15 pigs) for heat relief above 28Â°C, and evaporative cooling pads only in arid zones (Namibia, Botswana) where humidity is below 40%.

Heat stress above 26Â°C reduces feed intake by 15â30% and daily gain by 20%. Install a wall-mounted thermometer and hygrometer at pig height (0.6 m) in at least two locations per barn. Misting systems (1 nozzle per 10 pigs) reduce effective temperature by 3â5Â°C in dry heat.

Waste Management and Manure Handling

A 100-pig grow-finish unit produces 250â400 kg of manure per day. In Africa, the most profitable handling systems are: (1) deep litter with sawdust or maize cobs, composted and sold as organic fertiliser at USD 40â80 per tonne; (2) concrete manure channels flushed to a covered biogas digester â a 10 mÂ³ digester serves 50â80 pigs and produces 3â5 mÂ³ of biogas per day, enough for cooking for a family of six; (3) lagoon systems only where land is cheap and rainfall is low.

Never discharge raw slurry into waterways â it is a legal offence in Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa, and a biosecurity risk. Compost manure for 60 days at 55â65Â°C to kill pathogens and weed seeds before sale.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Biogas and Manure Gas

Manure pits, lagoons, and biogas digesters produce hydrogen sulphide (HâS), methane (CHâ), and ammonia (NHâ). HâS is lethal at concentrations above 500 ppm and can cause instant unconsciousness. Never enter a manure pit, lagoon, or digester without a harness, a second person standing by, and forced-air ventilation. Keep all flames and sparks away from biogas systems. Install gas detectors in enclosed manure handling areas. In 2022, a farm worker in Limpopo, South Africa, died after entering a slurry pit without respiratory protection â this is preventable.

Biosecurity Infrastructure and Layout

Biosecurity is the cheapest disease control you will ever buy. African Swine Fever (ASF) has wiped out entire herds in Uganda, Nigeria, and South Africa. Layout rules: single entry point with a vehicle wheel dip and footbath; perimeter fence 1.8 m high; 3 m clear zone between barns; shower-in/shower-out for staff and visitors; all-in/all-out batch flow with 7 days downtime between batches. Build a 2 m Ã 2 m changing room at the entrance with boots, overalls, and hand-wash station. Cost: USD 500â1,500 â less than the value of one sow.

Equipment for Feeding and Watering

Feeding: use stainless steel or concrete troughs for sows and wet-dry feeders for grow-finish pigs. Wet-dry feeders improve feed conversion by 5â8% and reduce water waste. Budget USD 25â60 per feeder for grow-finish. Watering: nipple drinkers at 1 per 10â12 pigs, flow rate 1.5â2 L/min for growers and 2â3 L/min for lactating sows. A lactating sow drinks 20â30 L/day; a finisher 6â10 L/day. Install a 5,000 L storage tank per 100 pigs and a pressure pump â water failure for 4 hours causes heat stress and reduced intake.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Farrowing pen: 2.4 m Ã 1.8 m with 0.6 mÂ² creep area heated to 30â32Â°C in week 1.
  2. Grow-finish barn: 8â10 m wide, 3.5â4 m ridge height, 1:6 roof pitch, 30â40 cm open ridge.
  3. Floor: concrete 8â10 cm thick, 2% slope to drain, raised 30â45 cm in high-rainfall zones.
  4. Ventilation: 0.6 mÂ³/min/pig max for growers; 1 fan per 15 pigs above 28Â°C.
  5. Manure: compost 60 days at 55â65Â°C, or feed a 10 mÂ³ biogas digester per 50â80 pigs.
  6. Biosecurity: single entry, wheel dip, footbath, shower-in, 3 m barn spacing, all-in/all-out.
  7. Water: 1 nipple per 10â12 pigs, 5,000 L tank per 100 pigs, 20â30 L/day per lactating sow.
  8. Never enter a manure pit or digester without harness, standby person, and forced ventilation.

Further Reading

  • South African Pork Producers' Organisation (SAPPO) â Housing and Environmental Guidelines
  • WOAH â African Swine Fever Biosecurity Guidance
  • Midwest Plan Service â Mechanical Ventilation Systems for Livestock Housing (MWPS-32)

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for a farrowing room for the sow?
quiz.explanation: Sows need a cool environment of 18-20Â°C to prevent heat stress, while piglets need a warmer creep area.

quiz.q: How much space does a grow-finish pig need in a fully slatted system?
quiz.explanation: Grow-finish pigs require 0.8-1.0 mÂ² per pig in slatted systems to reduce stress and fighting.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a creep area in a farrowing pen?
options: B) To provide a warm, safe area for piglets
D) To keep the sow cool
quiz.explanation: A creep area is a heated zone for piglets to rest away from the sow, reducing crushing.

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used for deep litter in pig barns?
quiz.explanation: Sawdust, wood shavings, or chopped straw are absorbent and commonly used for deep litter.

quiz.q: What is the recommended slope of a concrete floor in a pig pen?
quiz.explanation: A 1-2% slope allows proper drainage without being too slippery for pigs.

quiz.q: How many pigs can a 50-cm diameter fan ventilate?
quiz.explanation: A 50-cm fan moves about 10,000 mÂ³/hour, sufficient for 50-60 grow-finish pigs.

quiz.q: What is a sign of heat stress in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Pigs cannot sweat, so they pant to cool down when heat stressed.

quiz.q: What is the ideal humidity range for pig housing?
quiz.explanation: Humidity of 50-70% is comfortable for pigs; too high causes respiratory issues, too low causes dust.

quiz.q: How can you reduce ammonia levels in a pig barn?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia is a gas that builds up; increasing ventilation removes it.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ammonia level in a pig barn?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia should be below 20 ppm; higher levels irritate eyes and lungs.

quiz.q: How much manure does a pig produce per day?
quiz.explanation: A pig produces about 4-6 kg of manure daily, which is valuable but must be managed.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using a biogas digester for pig manure?
quiz.explanation: Biogas digesters convert manure into biogas, a renewable energy source for cooking and lighting.

quiz.q: How long should manure be composted before use?
quiz.explanation: Composting for 4-6 weeks kills pathogens and parasites, making manure safe for crops.

quiz.q: Why should fresh manure not be spread directly on fields?
options: B) It can burn plants and spread diseases
quiz.explanation: Fresh manure contains high ammonia and pathogens that can harm plants and spread disease.

quiz.q: How far should manure storage be from the pig barn?
quiz.explanation: A distance of at least 30 meters reduces flies and disease transmission.

quiz.q: What is the first line of defense in farm biosecurity?
quiz.explanation: A perimeter fence keeps out unauthorized people and animals, preventing disease entry.

quiz.q: What should be provided at the entrance of each pig building?
quiz.explanation: A footbath disinfects boots and prevents carrying pathogens into the barn.

quiz.q: How long should new pigs be quarantined?
quiz.explanation: A 30-day quarantine allows time for disease symptoms to appear before mixing with the herd.

quiz.q: What is the correct flow of movement in a pig farm?
options: D) From sick pen to nursery
quiz.explanation: Always move from clean areas (nursery) to dirty areas (grow-finish) to avoid spreading disease.

quiz.q: How should dead pigs be disposed of?
quiz.explanation: Burning or deep burial prevents disease spread and scavenger access.

quiz.q: What is the recommended space per piglet in a nursery?
quiz.explanation: Weaned piglets need 0.3-0.4 mÂ² each to grow well without stress.

quiz.q: How many pigs can one nipple drinker serve?
quiz.explanation: One nipple drinker is sufficient for 10-15 pigs, ensuring adequate water access.

quiz.q: At what height should a nipple drinker be for a grower pig?
quiz.explanation: Growers (10-20 weeks) need nipples at about 45 cm, at shoulder height.

quiz.q: How much water does a pig drink per day?
quiz.explanation: Pigs drink 5-10 liters daily, more in hot weather; water is essential for health.

quiz.q: What is a self-feeder?
options: A) A device that automatically feeds pigs
B) A pig that feeds itself
quiz.explanation: A self-feeder is a hopper that dispenses feed on demand, saving labor and reducing waste.

quiz.q: How much trough space should be provided per pig?
quiz.explanation: 20-30 cm of trough space per pig allows all pigs to eat without competition.

quiz.q: Why should feed be stored off the floor?
options: A) To prevent aflatoxin from moisture
B) To make it easier to reach
quiz.explanation: Storing feed on pallets prevents moisture absorption and mold growth, which produce aflatoxins.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to make a waterer from local materials?
options: A) A plastic drum with nipples
B) A clay pot with a lid
quiz.explanation: A plastic drum fitted with nipples is a low-cost, effective waterer for pigs.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean feed leftovers daily?
options: A) To prevent mold and disease
quiz.explanation: Leftover feed can grow mold and bacteria, causing illness; daily cleaning keeps feed fresh.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for a nursery piglet?
quiz.explanation: Nursery piglets need a warm environment of 26-28Â°C for optimal growth and health.
